current_example.title: Example: Finding a Jordan Decomposition of a 3x3 Matrix Given Its Two Distinct Eigenvalues

q-110560.name: Question 1
q-110560.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ -1 & 6 & 0 \\ -3 & 2 & 5\end{aligned}],\,J=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices above. Given that $A=PJ{P}^{-1}$ is a Jordan canonical decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the first column of the matrix $P?$

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,y=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,z=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]
$$
q-110560.worked_solution:
First, notice that the Jordan matrix $J$ may be written as a composition of Jordan blocks, as follows:

$$
J={J}_{2}(4)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(5)
$$

So, we have

- one $2\times 2$ Jordan block corresponding to $\lambda =4,$ and

- one $1\times 1$ Jordan block corresponding to $\lambda =5.$

Therefore, the columns of $P$ form the following chains: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{2}(4) & : & {v}_{2}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {J}_{1}(5) & : & {v}_{3}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

As a result, the first column of $P$ is an eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda =4.$ 

Now, computing $A-4I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ -1 & 6 & 0 \\ -3 & 2 & 5\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & 0 \\ -3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Among the given vectors, only 
$z$
is an eigenvector of $A,$ since

$$
(A-4I)z=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & 0 \\ -3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],
$$

and we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0.\end{aligned}
$$

The other vectors do not satisfy this condition.

q-110554.name: Question 2
q-110554.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ -4 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}],\,J=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices above. Given that $A=PJ{P}^{-1}$ is a Jordan canonical decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the first column of the matrix $P?$

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,y=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,z=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$
q-110554.worked_solution:
First, notice that the Jordan matrix $J$ may be written as a composition of Jordan blocks, as follows:

$$
J={J}_{2}(-2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(1)
$$

So, we have

- one $2\times 2$ Jordan block corresponding to $\lambda =-2,$ and

- one $1\times 1$ Jordan block corresponding to $\lambda =1.$

Therefore, the columns of $P$ form the following chains: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{2}(-2) & : & {v}_{2}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {J}_{1}(1) & : & {v}_{3}\overset{A-I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

As a result, the first column of $P$ is an eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda =-2.$ 

Now, computing $A+2I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+2I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ -4 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 4 & 0 \\ -4 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Among the given vectors, only 
$z$
is an eigenvector of $A,$ since

$$
(A+2I)z=[\begin{aligned}4 & 4 & 0 \\ -4 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],
$$

and we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0.\end{aligned}
$$

The other vectors do not satisfy this condition.

q-109679.name: Question 3
q-109679.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 3 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}],\,J=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices above. Given that $A=PJ{P}^{-1}$ is a Jordan canonical decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the second column of the matrix $P?$

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,y=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,z=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$
q-109679.worked_solution:
First, notice that the Jordan matrix $J$ may be written as a composition of Jordan blocks, as follows:

$$
J={J}_{2}(2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(2)
$$

So, we have

- one $2\times 2$ Jordan block corresponding to $\lambda =2,$ and

- one $1\times 1$ Jordan block corresponding to $\lambda =2.$

Therefore, the columns of $P$ form the following chains: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{2}(2) & : & {v}_{2}\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {J}_{1}(2) & : & {v}_{3}\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

As a result, the second column of $P$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to $\lambda =2.$ 

Now, computing $A-2I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 3 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Among the given vectors, only $y$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2,$ since

$$
(A-2I)y=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=x,
$$

and, therefore,

$$
(A-2I)^{2}y=(A-2I)x=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],
$$

and we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }0.\end{aligned}
$$

The other vectors do not satisfy this condition.

q-110701.name: Question 4
q-110701.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 5 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 4\end{aligned}],\,J=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices above. Given that $A=PJ{P}^{-1}$ is a Jordan canonical decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the second column of the matrix $P?$

$$

$$
q-110701.worked_solution:
First, notice that the Jordan matrix $J$ may be written as a composition of Jordan blocks, as follows:

$$
J={J}_{2}(4)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(4)
$$

So, we have

- one $2\times 2$ Jordan block corresponding to $\lambda =4,$ and

- one $1\times 1$ Jordan block corresponding to $\lambda =4.$

Therefore, the columns of $P$ form the following chains: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{2}(4) & : & {v}_{2}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {J}_{1}(4) & : & {v}_{3}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

As a result, the second column of $P$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to $\lambda =4.$ 

Now, computing $A-4I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 5 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 4\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Among the given vectors, only $z$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2,$ since

$$
(A-4I)z=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=y,
$$

and, therefore,

$$
(A-4I)^{2}z=(A-4I)y=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0.\end{aligned}
$$

q-110591.name: Question 6
q-110591.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & -5 & 4\end{aligned}],\,J=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}∗ & 0 & a \\ ∗ & 1 & b \\ ∗ & 2 & c\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices above. Given that $A=PJ{P}^{-1}$ is a Jordan canonical decomposition of $A,$ find the value of $a+c.$
q-110591.worked_solution:
Since the Jordan block $J$ has a single $3\times 3$ Jordan block corresponding to $\lambda =2,$ the columns of $P$ form the following chain: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{3}\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }{v}_{2}\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }0\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we obtain that 

- the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvector ${v}_{1}$ of the eigenvalue $\lambda =2,$

- the second column of $P$ corresponds to the vector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ such that $(A-2I){v}_{2}={v}_{1},$

- the third column of $P$ corresponds to the vector ${v}_{3}$ such that $(A-2I){v}_{3}={v}_{2}.$

Now, computing $A-2I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & -5 & 4\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -5 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, the matrix equation $(A-2I){v}_{3}={v}_{2}$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -5 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & -5 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we have ${x}_{2}=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}-2\cdot 0+{x}_{3}=1\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=1-{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}1-{x}_{3} \\ 0 \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get  

$$
{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a+c=0+1=1.$

- the second column of $P$ corresponds to the vector ${v}_{2}$ such that $(A-4I){v}_{2}={v}_{1}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

Finally, $2a+b=2\cdot 1+(-1)=1.$

$$

$$

So, we have

- a single $2\times 2$ Jordan block corresponding to $\lambda =5,$ and

- a single $1\times 1$ block corresponding to $\lambda =-2.$

Therefore, the columns of $P$ form the following chains: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{2}(5) & : & {v}_{2}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {J}_{1}(-2) & : & {v}_{3}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we obtain that 

- the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]$ of the eigenvalue $\lambda =5,$

- the second column of $P$ corresponds to the vector ${v}_{2}$ such that $(A-5I){v}_{2}={v}_{1}.$

Now, computing $A-5I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ -14 & -16 & -2\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -14 & -16 & -7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, the matrix equation $(A-5I){v}_{2}={v}_{1}$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -14 & -16 & -7 & -2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3} \\ {R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-14 & -16 & -7 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we have ${x}_{2}=1.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
-14{x}_{1}-16\cdot 1-7{x}_{3}=-2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3}-1.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3}-1 \\ 1 \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{3}=0,$ we get  

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $2a+c=2\cdot (-1)+0=-2.$

- the second column of $P$ corresponds to the vector ${v}_{2}$ such that $(A-I){v}_{2}={v}_{1}.$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & -2 \\ -1 & -1 & 0 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 & 7\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
